passage: I'm Lakshmi, and from the next balcony I watch Uday, who is two, open every drawer in his kitchen. He pulled out spoons, sniffed a steel bowl and put a fallen leaf in his mouth. His mother calmly took the leaf and said, "Leaf's not for eating." She moved the knives higher and put pots in the bottom drawer. Uday banged them, delighted. I can't know what he thinks, but he looked thrilled.

qa.q: What did Uday put in his mouth?
qa.a: Uday put a fallen leaf in his mouth.

qa.q: What was Uday probably feeling as he banged the pots?
qa.a: Uday seemed delighted and thrilled, though Lakshmi cannot know for certain what he was thinking.

qa.q: What did Uday's mother do that worked better than only saying no?
qa.a: She calmly took the leaf, moved the knives higher and put pots in the bottom drawer, so his exploring was safe and welcome.

qa.q: How might Uday's mother have felt watching him open every drawer?
qa.a: She probably felt watchful and a bit tired, but calm. She chose to make the kitchen safe instead of scolding.

grounding: A toddler opens drawers, mouths a leaf and pulls things around; safety-proofing works better than constant no, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday: Omkar, two, opened every drawer while his mother Ganga said "No, no" all day. Wednesday: Ganga locked the knife drawer and gave him the bottom one, filled with steel cups and wooden spoons. Saturday: Omkar dragged each thing out, tasted a spoon and banged a cup, and played for half an hour while Ganga cooked, no longer saying no.

qa.q: Which drawer did Ganga give Omkar?
qa.a: Ganga gave Omkar the bottom drawer, filled with steel cups and wooden spoons.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling on Saturday as he banged the cup?
qa.a: Omkar was absorbed and happy, playing for half an hour on his own.

qa.q: What change made the difference between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: Ganga locked the dangerous drawer and gave Omkar a safe one to explore, so the day stopped being a string of no's.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt on Monday compared with Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday Ganga was probably worn out and anxious from saying no all day. On Saturday Ganga was calmer and able to cook.

grounding: A toddler opens drawers and tastes things; safety-proofing works better than constant saying no, shown across three days.

passage: In Aji's house in the village, Tushar, two, pulled open every tin on the low shelf. Rice spilled. Lentils rolled. He tasted a neem leaf, made a face and spat. His aunt Jaya laughed. She moved the kerosene can and the matches up high. Then she filled a basket with steel bowls, a wooden spoon and a clean cloth. "Here, Tushar. These are yours." He banged the bowls, stacked them, and tipped them over again and again, shrieking with joy.

qa.q: What did Tushar taste?
qa.a: He tasted a neem leaf.

qa.q: How can you tell Tushar felt happy with the basket?
qa.a: He banged, stacked and tipped the bowls again and again, shrieking with joy.

qa.q: Why did Jaya's approach work better than saying no?
qa.a: She moved dangerous things up high and gave him safe things to explore, so his curiosity could keep going safely.

qa.q: How might Aji feel about the spilled rice and lentils?
qa.a: Aji might be a little tired of cleaning up, but glad Tushar is safe and busy.

grounding: Shows a toddler opening tins and tasting leaves, and an adult making the space safe instead of saying no.

passage: In their small flat in Lisbon, Mei, eighteen months old, found a pinecone and pulled it apart scale by scale. Then she opened the cupboard under the sink. Ines, her mother, gently closed it and snapped on a child latch. She opened the bottom drawer instead and filled it with plastic cups, a whisk and a scarf. Mei crawled over, pulled everything out, put the whisk in her mouth, then waved the scarf like a flag. She laughed and looked up at Ines, as if to say, "Look what I found!"

qa.q: What did Mei pull apart scale by scale?
qa.a: A pinecone.

qa.q: What does Mei looking up at Ines and laughing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mei felt delighted and proud of her discoveries and wanted to share them with her mother.

qa.q: What did Ines do that made exploring safe?
qa.a: She latched the cupboard under the sink and filled a low drawer with safe things for Mei to explore.

qa.q: How might Ines feel watching Mei with the drawer?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and happy that Mei can explore freely without danger.

grounding: Shows a toddler exploring by pulling things apart and mouthing them, and a parent safety-proofing instead of constantly saying no.

passage:
Monday: Payal, two, opened every kitchen drawer. "No! No, Payal!" said Papa Ojas, again and again. She cried and tried again.
Wednesday: Papa put locks on the knife and medicine drawers. He made one low drawer "Payal's drawer," with lids, spoons and a squishy ball.
Saturday: Payal opened her drawer, took out every lid, tasted one, and banged two together. She laughed. Papa sat on the floor and banged a spoon with her. Nobody said no all morning.

qa.q: What did Papa put locks on?
qa.a: The knife and medicine drawers.

qa.q: How did Payal feel on Saturday compared to Monday?
qa.a: On Monday she was upset and crying; on Saturday she was happy and laughing as she explored her own drawer.

qa.q: What small change made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Locking the dangerous drawers and making a safe 'Payal's drawer', so Papa didn't need to keep saying no.

qa.q: How did the change affect Papa?
qa.a: Papa could relax and play with Payal, banging a spoon with her instead of saying no all morning.

grounding: Shows a toddler's drawer-opening curiosity and how safety-proofing worked better than repeatedly saying no.

passage: Yogesh, nearly two, had opened every kitchen drawer in the flat. He licked a spoon and tore the pages off an old calendar. On the balcony he stuffed a tulsi leaf into his mouth and made a face. His father, Mridul, had stopped saying "No!" every minute. Instead he had tied the knife drawer shut, moved the cleaning bottles up high, and filled the lowest drawer with lids and spoons, just for Yogesh.

qa.q: Which drawer did Mridul tie shut?
qa.a: He tied the knife drawer shut.

qa.q: What do Yogesh's drawer-opening and leaf-tasting suggest he feels?
qa.a: He seems curious and excited 😊 wanting to find out what everything is, feels like and tastes like.

qa.q: Which of Mridul's choices works better than saying no, and why?
qa.a: Filling a low drawer with lids and spoons, because it gives Yogesh something safe to explore instead of just stopping him.

qa.q: What would change if Mridul kept saying "No!" every minute?
qa.a: Yogesh might get frustrated, Mridul would be worn out, and the dangerous things would still be within reach.

grounding: Shows a toddler exploring by opening, tasting and pulling things apart, and a parent childproofing instead of constantly saying no.
